idiom_name: Ktor CachingHeaders plugin plus a Caffeine-backed page store (or Spring Boot @Cacheable)
implementation_notes: Ktor ships the metadata half only: install(CachingHeaders) { options { call, content -> ... } } writes Cache-Control/Expires per content type, but no page is stored, so the bytes live in a cache such as Caffeine (maximumSize + expireAfterWrite) behind a small route interceptor or plugin that keys on method, URI and the vary axes and answers hits without invoking the handler. On the Spring Boot side of the JVM the same pattern is declarative: @Cacheable on the suspend/service function that assembles the page, backed by a CacheManager, with the response headers set separately. In both realizations the store is per-JVM unless a distributed provider is plugged in, so eviction, TTL and purge come from Caffeine's policy or the shared cache, not from Ktor.
pitfalls: CachingHeaders only writes headers: assuming it caches the page leaves the origin running on every request while clients happily serve stale copies.
Caffeine is per-process and evicts by policy: size the cache and expect recomputes, or the page cache competes with the JVM heap and produces GC pressure instead of relief.
Coroutine handlers must not hold an entry lock across suspension points; use Caffeine's async loading (or another single-flight mechanism) rather than double-checked locking in suspend code.
